title: Dimensions and determinants of judgements of colour samples and a simulated interior space by architects and non-architects
authors: J. Hogg, S. Goodman, T. Porter, B. Mikellides and D. E. Preddy, 1979
research_question: To identify the dimensions and determinants of colour judgements for colour chips and a simulated interior space, and to compare these judgements between architects and non-architects, relating them to Munsell colour system coordinates.

participants.description: 10 architect subjects (qualified architects and architecture students, mean age 26, 5 male/5 female) and 10 non-architect subjects (professional people e.g., librarians, lighting engineers, social workers, mean age 33, 5 male/5 female).

stimuli_or_exposures.description: 44 semi-matt colour chips (12mm x 17mm) selected from the BSI Range (Munsell-based) across five major hue groups (red, yellow, green, blue, purple), including black and white. Chosen for approximately equal chroma and value representation across hue groups and adequate sampling across the range.

A model of a room space (560mm x 280mm x 900mm) with the coloured panel representing the end wall. Floor and side walls painted grey (Munsell N7; 00 A 05), ceiling covered with fine white gauze for light transmission. The end wall was grey when no coloured panel was present. Panels viewed at 1000mm, chips at 600mm. Illumination: 260 lux from artificial daylight tubes, 30 candelas/m² on end wall/chip from suspended tube, colour rendering index 95.

measures.instrument: 24 Semantic Differential scales (e.g., exciting-calming, open-closed, cold-hot, dynamic-static, hard-soft, vibrant-still, austere-lush, modern-traditional, unusual-usual, complex-simple, pleasant-unpleasant, fresh-stale, weak-strong, cramped-spacious, blatant-muted, controlled-uncontrolled, obvious-subtle, free-constricted, active-passive, introverted-extraverted, dull-sharp, private-public, receptive-repellent, loose-tight). Ratings qualified with 'neutral', 'slightly', 'moderately', 'extremely'.
Principal components analysis with varimax rotation on 24x24 product moment correlation matrices of scale ratings.

measures.construct: Relation of factor dimensions to colour attributes
measures.instrument: Product moment correlations between factor loadings and Munsell hue, value, and chroma quantifications. Isosemantic maps for graphical illustration of non-linear relations.

findings.consequent: Judgements of dynamism (more dynamic) for colour chips (total sample)
findings.mechanism: As chroma increased, colours were judged as being more dynamic.

findings.consequent: Judgements of spatial quality (more spacious) for colour chips (total sample)
findings.mechanism: As colour value increased, it was considered more spacious.

findings.consequent: Judgements of emotional tone (cooler, harder, more austere) for colour chips (total sample)
findings.mechanism: Colours decreased in emotional tone (became cooler, harder, and more austere) round the hue circle from red to purple.

findings.consequent: Judgements of emotional tone (higher emotional tone) for colour chips (total sample)
findings.mechanism: Decreasing chroma enhanced the effect of hue on emotional tone (i.e., higher chroma associated with higher emotional tone).

findings.antecedent: Colour chroma (low) AND colour value (high or low)
findings.consequent: Judgements of dynamism (more dynamic) for colour chips (total sample)
findings.mechanism: Isosemantic maps show that high or low value may compensate for low chroma, increasing dynamism.
findings.quote: The bowed effect of the contours, particularly clear for the red, green, blue and purple maps, indicates that high or low value may compensate for low chroma.

findings.antecedent: Colour chroma (increasing) AND hue (green, blue, purple)
findings.consequent: Judgements of spatial quality (increasing spaciousness) for colour chips (total sample)
findings.mechanism: For green, blue, and purple maps, increasing chroma generally leads to an increase in spaciousness.
findings.quote: For the green, blue, and purple maps, increasing chroma generally leads to an increase in spaciousness.

findings.antecedent: Colour chroma (increasing from value axis) AND hue (yellow, red)
findings.consequent: Judgements of spatial quality (increases then decreases) for colour chips (total sample)
findings.mechanism: For yellow, the relation of spaciousness to chroma is curvilinear. As chroma increases from the value axis, spaciousness increases, then decreases. For red, the effect of chroma is similar to that of yellow.
findings.quote: For yellow, the relation of spaciousness to chroma is curvilinear. As chroma increases from the value axis, spaciousness increases, then decreases.

findings.antecedent: Colour chroma (low) AND colour value (low or high)
findings.consequent: Judgements of complexity (simple) for colour chips (total sample)
findings.mechanism: Colours of low chroma, but of low or high value, are judged as simple.
findings.quote: Colours of low chroma, but of low or high value, are judged as simple.

findings.consequent: Judgements of complexity (complex) for colour chips (total sample)
findings.mechanism: Complex colours are generally of medium value.
findings.quote: Complex colours are generally of medium value.

findings.consequent: Judgements of evaluation (preferred or neutral) for models (total sample)
findings.mechanism: Yellow and Blue maps indicate these hues are in the main preferred, or judged as neutral.
findings.quote: The Yellow and Blue maps both indicate that these hues are in the main preferred, or judged as neutral.

findings.consequent: Judgements of evaluation (low preference or neutrality) for models (total sample)
findings.mechanism: Green and purple maps show predominantly low preference or neutrality.
findings.quote: In contrast, the green and purple maps show predominantly low preference or neutrality.

findings.antecedent: Colour hue (red) AND colour value (high) AND colour chroma (medium and low)
findings.consequent: Judgements of evaluation (unpleasant) for models (total sample)
findings.mechanism: High values of red in medium and low chromas are predominantly unpleasant.
findings.quote: e.g. high values of red in medium and low chromas are predominantly unpleasant.

findings.consequent: Factor structure of judgements (marked difference for Factor IV - Evaluation)
findings.mechanism: For non-architects, pleasant-unpleasant and receptive-repellent loaded on Factor I (Dynamism) for colour chips, unlike architects where it loaded on Factor IV (Evaluation).
findings.quote: However, in judgements of colour chips and models by non-architects, there is a marked difference from the architects in factor IV.

findings.consequent: Determinants of evaluation for models (striking differences in preferred/not preferred colours)
findings.mechanism: Architects associated 'pleasant' and 'receptive' with 'modern' and 'controlled', while non-architects associated these with 'fresh' and 'lush'.
findings.quote: However, when the preferences of architects and non-architects for models are compared, striking differences in which colours are preferred and not preferred emerged.

findings.consequent: Judgements of dynamism
findings.mechanism: The most striking point of comparison relates to the influence of chroma on dynamism and like factors.
findings.quote: The most striking point of comparison relates to the influence of chroma on dynamism and like factors

findings.consequent: Judgements of emotional tone
findings.mechanism: The most striking point of comparison relates to the influence of hue on emotional tone.

findings.consequent: Judgements of spatial quality
findings.mechanism: The most striking point of comparison relates to the influence of value on spatial quality.
findings.quote: and possibly value on spatial quality.

findings.consequent: Judgements of evaluation or preference
findings.mechanism: For the recurrent dimension of evaluation or preference, differences emerge in the determinants, and typically evaluation does not have any obvious linear correlates.
findings.quote: Typically, evaluation does not have any obvious linear correlates.

mechanisms: Linear correlations between colour parameters (chroma, value, hue) and specific judgement factors (dynamism, spatial quality, emotional tone) suggest inherent, possibly biological, relations between colour attributes and their connotations.
Non-linear and interactive effects, particularly for complexity and evaluation, suggest the influence of learning, culture, or training.

Differences in evaluative judgements between architects and non-architects, especially for models, indicate that professional training or cultural background can modulate preference, even when other perceptual dimensions are similar.
moderators: Stimuli type (colour chips vs. models of interior space)
implementation_implications: The consistent relationships between colour attributes and dynamism, spatial quality, and emotional tone across different groups and contexts suggest fundamental principles for colour use in design.

The divergence in evaluative judgements between architects and non-architects, especially in a spatial context, highlights the importance of considering user groups when designing for preference or aesthetic appeal.

limitations: Variations in the choice of scales limit direct comparison with other studies.
Studies of biological response to colour and the influence of associative/learning factors are not available in a form that would allow further inferences on the proposed hypothesis.
Previous physiological work on colour has typically limited itself to a small number of colours, varying only in hue, and has not provided clear support for Goldstein's position.
Studies of learning effects on colour response are few and limited to demonstrations of operant and classical conditioning.

paper_metadata.title: Dimensions and determinants of judgements of colour samples and a simulated interior space by architects and non-architects.
paper_metadata.crossref_title: Dimensions and determinants of judgements of colour samples and a simulated interior space by architects and non‐architects
paper_metadata.crossref_abstract:
Architects and non‐architects made Semantic Differential ratings of colour samples (chips) and a simulated interior space (a model). In analyses of total samples’ ratings (architects and non‐architects) of (a) colour chips and (b) models, and individual sample analyses, (c) architects’ chip judgements, (d) architects’ model judgements, (e) non‐architects’ chip judgements, and (f) non‐architects’ model judgements, five factors occurred, though not necessarily all in any one analysis. These were: (i) dynamism; (ii) spatial quality; (iii) emotional tone; (iv) evaluation; (v) complexity. Linear correlations between parameters of Munsell Color System and above factors in various analyses were calculated, while parallel analyses were carried out employing a graphical technique described by Sivik (1974
                    a
                    ) involving isosemantic maps. In all analyses, linear correlations between colour parameters and judgements were found for dynamism factor, spatial quality factor, and emotional tone factor. They were associated respectively with chroma, value, and hue. Inspection of isosemantic maps indicated subsidiary effects of non‐dominant dimensions of a non‐linear sort, though maps also exhibited linear relations. Linear correlations were low or non‐existent for evaluation and complexity factors, and complex nature of their determinants was clear from isosemantic maps. determinants of judgements were similar for architects and non‐architects, with exception of evaluative judgements for models in which markedly different determinants were noted.
                  
                  Comparability of present findings with other studies carried out in a variety of countries over a 20 year period was high for dynamism, spatial quality, and emotional tone, and it is suggested that there may be something inherent in response to colour in relation to such judgements. Recent physiological work is discussed, and its limitations in terms of colours sampled and an overconcentration on hue dimension noted. In contrast, it is suggested that dimensions of judgement, such as evaluation or complexity, reflect to a greater extent culture or training, and are hence independent of basic colour attributes.
